title: Imagined experience under ablation
takeaway: Suppressing the J-space while the model imagines what a moment is like for another person collapses its experiential language score on Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, and Opus 4.6, while matched-norm control perturbations leave the score near baseline. The flattening effect is therefore not specific to the model describing itself; the paper reads the J-space as supporting rich experiential description as such.
walkthrough:
The figure closes the experiential-report experiments. The earlier figure in this section asked the model to narrate its own stream of consciousness. This one points the prompts outward. The model is asked to imagine what a specific moment is like for a person — someone who has just opened a letter from someone they have not heard from in years, or someone waiting by the phone for news they are dreading. The figure answers whether the [[experiential-report-flattening]] effect is specific to self-description.

The left side holds a representative pair of responses from Sonnet 4.5 to the same imagination prompt: one from the unmodified model, one under [[j-space-ablation]]. In the article this panel is a live widget, so the transcripts can be read in full rather than as excerpts. The ablation projects out, at every position across layers L38–54, the [[residual-stream]]'s components along the ten most active [[j-lens-vector]] directions. That is the lightest setting from the self-report experiment — larger $k$ or later layers damage coherence before anything else changes.

The right side is the quantitative summary: the [[experiential-language-score]], plotted by model and condition. The score is the mean of three binary judgments by an [[llm-grader]] — whether the response conveys the moment from the inside, whether it speaks from a felt first-person perspective, and whether its vocabulary is sensory rather than computational. The models are Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, and Opus 4.6 from the [[claude-model-family]]; Haiku 4.5 is left out because ablation breaks its coherence before its register changes. The conditions are the unablated baseline, J-space ablation, and [[matched-norm-controls]]: perturbations of the same magnitude, at the same layers and positions, but along a random direction, against the non-J-space component, or against the most aligned [[sparse-autoencoder]] decoder directions. Error bars are 95% intervals; dots are per-prompt rates.

The pattern repeats the self-report result. Under ablation the score collapses on all three models, and the controls stay near baseline. The ablated responses remain detailed and remain about the person, but they read more like event logs than like descriptions of experience. A separate [[story-writing-control]] shows this is not a general loss of writing ability. The paper's reading is that the J-space supports the propensity to give rich experiential reports, whether the subject is the model or someone else.

terms.definition: The intervention under test: at each token position, the residual stream's projections onto the top-10 most active J-lens vectors are removed, suppressing the workspace's current contents wholesale.

Control interventions calibrated to perturb the activations by the same magnitude as J-space ablation, at the same layers and token positions, but along other directions: a random direction, the non-J-space component, or aligned SAE decoder directions.

The y-axis quantity: the average of three binary LLM-graded judgments of whether a response describes the moment from the inside — felt rather than observed, first-person felt rather than third-person mechanism, sensory rather than computational vocabulary.
The unperturbed condition: the same imagination prompt with no intervention on the activations, giving the model's ordinary experiential register.
The mid-size Claude model whose representative baseline and ablated responses fill the figure's left panel, and one of the three models in the score comparison.
A larger Claude model included in the score comparison; it shows the same collapse under ablation.
The most recent large Claude model in the comparison; it too shows the collapse. A model of this tier also serves as the grader behind the score.
The smallest model tier, absent from the figure: on Haiku 4.5, J-space ablation degrades coherence before producing any qualitative change in the responses.
The grouping on the score panel: baseline, J-space ablation, and each matched-norm control, so the ablation's effect can be read against same-magnitude perturbations.

The prompt family for this figure: requests to describe the subjective experience of a person in a specific moment, such as opening a letter from someone not heard from in years, or waiting by the phone for dreaded news.
The layer range over which the ablation acts, written in the paper's percent-of-depth indexing; it is the first third of the workspace layer range.
The per-token vocabulary-aligned vectors of the Jacobian lens; the ten most active of them at each position define what the ablation removes.
A control that perturbs the activation along a random direction with the same norm the ablation would have removed at that layer and position.
A control that shrinks the part of the activation lying outside the J-space by the matched amount, testing whether removing anything of that size flattens the reports.
A control that dampens the activation's projections onto its ten most strongly aligned sparse-autoencoder decoder directions, a same-size perturbation along interpretable but non-lens features.
95% confidence intervals on the average score per model and condition; the paper's proportion error bars use the Wilson interval.
Per-prompt score rates overlaid on each bar, showing the spread across the individual imagination prompts behind the average.
A language model scoring responses against a written rubric in place of human raters; here Opus 4.6 answers the three binary questions that make up the score.

numbers.meaning: The number of most active J-lens directions projected out at each token position. Larger values of k tend to impair the coherence of responses, so the paper stays at 10.

The layer range the ablation covers — the first third of the workspace range in the paper's 0–100 percent-of-depth indexing. Later layer ranges, like larger k, tend to break coherence before changing the register.
Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, and Opus 4.6 appear in the score panel. Haiku 4.5 is excluded because ablation degrades its coherence before any qualitative change appears.
The experiential language score averages three binary grader judgments (felt versus observed, first-person felt perspective, sensory vocabulary), so each response scores 0, 1/3, 2/3, or 1.

The main comparison uses three matched-norm perturbations: a random direction, shrinking the non-J-space component, and dampening the top-10 aligned SAE decoder directions. Each is calibrated to the ablation's perturbation magnitude at the same layer and position.
The confidence level of the error bars on each average score, computed as Wilson intervals for proportions.
The range of the experiential language score: 0 means all three graders judged the response non-experiential, 1 means all three judged it experiential.

The section names two representative imagination prompts — the letter from someone not heard from in years, and waiting by the phone for dreaded news; the figure shows one representative response pair from the set.
